name: Neurocritical Care
sub: TBI, ICP, stroke, status epilepticus, brain death, delirium

cards.q: What are the ICP treatment thresholds and CPP targets in severe TBI?
cards.a: Treat ICP >22 mmHg (BTF 4th edition). Target cerebral perfusion pressure 60–70 mmHg; avoid aggressive attempts to push CPP above 70.
cards.src: Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed. (2016; 5th edition in preparation)

cards.q: Outline the tiered management of raised ICP.
cards.a: Tier 0: head up 30°, neutral neck, treat pain, agitation, fever and hypoxia. Tier 1: sedation, hyperosmolar therapy (3% saline or mannitol), CSF drainage. Tier 2: brief hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 30–35 as a bridge, deeper sedation, mild hypothermia. Tier 3: barbiturate coma or decompressive craniectomy.

cards.q: What are the doses of mannitol and hypertonic saline for raised ICP?
cards.a: Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg IV over 15–20 min (serum osmolality <320 mOsm/kg). 3% saline 2–5 mL/kg bolus or 23.4% 30 mL via central line; target sodium 145–155 mmol/L.

cards.q: What is the Cushing reflex?
cards.a: Hypertension (widened pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular respiration in response to markedly raised ICP and brainstem compression.

cards.q: What is the Monro–Kellie doctrine?
cards.a: The cranial vault is a fixed volume containing brain, blood and CSF; an increase in one compartment must be offset by a decrease in another or ICP rises.

cards.q: What is the time window for IV thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke?
cards.a: Alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of last known well; disabling deficits are treated quickly without advanced-imaging selection. Selected patients with unknown onset or 4.5–9 hours may be treated if advanced imaging is favourable (e.g. DWI-FLAIR or perfusion mismatch). For non-disabling deficits, DAPT is preferred over thrombolysis. BP before and after lysis: use the guideline limits (AHA 2019 values were <185/110 before and <180/105 after; confirm in the 2026 full text). Thrombectomy is standard for large-vessel occlusion, now extended to some larger cores, and basilar occlusion within 24 hours with NIHSS ≥10.

cards.q: How is intracerebral haemorrhage managed acutely?
cards.a: Targeted SBP lowering (about 140 mmHg; avoid <130), reverse anticoagulants (PCC and vitamin K for warfarin; idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors), neurosurgical consultation, ICP management.

cards.q: Outline the management of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage.
cards.a: Secure the aneurysm early (<24–72 h) by coiling or clipping, nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days, maintain euvolaemia, avoid hypotension, and screen for vasospasm (days 4–14), hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia.

cards.q: What is the Hunt–Hess / WFNS grading used for?
cards.a: Grading clinical severity of subarachnoid haemorrhage; WFNS uses GCS and motor deficit. Higher grades predict worse outcome and vasospasm risk.

cards.q: Outline the stepwise treatment of status epilepticus.
cards.a: 0–5 min: stabilise, check glucose. 5–20 min: benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, IM midazolam 10 mg, or IV diazepam). 20–40 min: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg. >40 min: anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, thiopental) with EEG monitoring.

cards.q: What did ESETT show?
cards.a: Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate had similar efficacy (about 45–47% seizure cessation) as second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus.

cards.q: What are the clinical prerequisites before brain death testing?
cards.a: A known irreversible cause of catastrophic brain injury, exclusion of confounders (sedatives, neuromuscular blockade, hypothermia <36 °C, severe metabolic or endocrine derangement, hypotension), and normal temperature and MAP ≥60–65 mmHg.

cards.q: List the brainstem reflexes tested in brain-death assessment.
cards.a: Pupillary light, corneal, oculocephalic (doll's eye), oculovestibular (cold caloric), cough and gag reflexes, absent motor response to pain, and apnoea testing (PaCO₂ rise to ≥60 mmHg or 20 above baseline with pH <7.30).

cards.q: What is the physiology and management of neurogenic diabetes insipidus in the brain-dead donor?
cards.a: Loss of ADH causing polyuria with hypernatraemia; treat with desmopressin 1–4 mcg IV or vasopressin infusion and replace free water.

cards.q: What are the aims of temperature control after cardiac arrest?
cards.a: Prevent fever and secondary brain injury. AHA 2025: goal 32–37.5 °C, maintained at least 36 hours in patients not following commands. ERC-ESICM 2025 now says temperature control and actively prevents fever (≤37.5 °C) for 36–72 hours. TTM2 found no benefit of 33 °C over normothermia with fever control.

cards.q: How do you assess delirium in ICU?
cards.a: Use a validated tool such as CAM-ICU or ICDSC (acute onset, inattention, disorganised thinking or altered level of consciousness). Prevent with early mobilisation, sleep promotion, minimal benzodiazepines and family involvement. PADIS 2025 makes no recommendation for or against antipsychotics to treat delirium.

cards.q: What is the Glasgow Coma Scale and the best motor responses?
cards.a: Eye (1–4), verbal (1–5) and motor (1–6) responses; motor: obeys 6, localises 5, withdraws 4, abnormal flexion 3, extension 2, none 1.

cards.q: What is the difference between a central and nephrogenic cause of polyuria with hypernatraemia after neurosurgery?
cards.a: Central DI responds to desmopressin with a rise in urine osmolality; nephrogenic does not. Cerebral salt wasting, in contrast, causes hyponatraemia with volume depletion and high urine sodium.

cards.q: What are the principles of managing Guillain–Barré syndrome in ICU?
cards.a: Monitor FVC and negative inspiratory force (intubate if FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF worse than −30 cmH₂O or bulbar weakness), autonomic monitoring, IVIG 0.4 g/kg for 5 days or plasma exchange, and thromboprophylaxis.

cards.q: What are the features of myasthenic crisis and its management?
cards.a: Bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness precipitated by infection, surgery or drugs. Support ventilation, avoid precipitating drugs (aminoglycosides, magnesium), start IVIG or plasma exchange; hold cholinesterase inhibitors while intubated.

cards.q: A patient with severe TBI has ICP 28 mmHg despite sedation and head elevation. What is the most appropriate next step?
cards.e: Hyperosmolar therapy is a first-line medical step. Steroids are harmful in TBI (CRASH) and extreme hypothermia is unproven.

cards.q: A 40-year-old has had a generalised seizure for 25 minutes despite 8 mg IV lorazepam. What is the next treatment?
o: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin or valproate IV
cards.e: Established status epilepticus requires a second-line anticonvulsant. If refractory after 40 minutes, move to anaesthetic infusion.

cards.q: What are the main changes in the 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischaemic stroke guideline?
cards.a: Mobile stroke units endorsed; tenecteplase or alteplase within 4.5 h; extended-window thrombolysis (unknown onset or 4.5–9 h) in selected patients with advanced imaging; DAPT preferred over thrombolysis for non-disabling deficits; thrombectomy broadened to some larger cores and basilar occlusion within 24 h (NIHSS ≥10); do not delay thrombectomy to judge the response to thrombolysis; no adjunctive argatroban or eptifibatide with IVT; do not lower SBP intensively to <140 mmHg after reperfusion; do not target glucose 80–130 mg/dL.

cards.q: What are the five statements in the 2025 PADIS focused update?
cards.a: Anxiety: insufficient evidence on benzodiazepines (no recommendation). Sedation: dexmedetomidine suggested over propofol in ventilated adults when light sedation or less delirium is the priority. Delirium: no recommendation for or against antipsychotics. Immobility: enhanced mobilisation and rehabilitation suggested. Sleep: melatonin suggested (low certainty).
